Indoors means inside a building. When you do something indoors, you are doing it within an enclosed structure that has walls and a roof — like a house, school, office, gym, restaurant, or mall.

Think of it this way: a building separates the world into two zones — the space inside it, and the space outside it. "Indoors" refers to being or doing something in that inside zone.

We stayed indoors because it was raining.
(= We stayed inside the building because it was raining.)
What Kind of Word Is It, and How Does It Work?

As an adverb, "indoors" describes where an action takes place. It answers the question "Where?" It attaches to a verb and tells you the location of that action.

She went indoors.
(Where did she go? — Indoors. It modifies the verb "went.")

The children played indoors all afternoon.
(Where did they play? — Indoors. It modifies the verb "played.")

The wedding was held indoors due to the storm.
(Where was it held? — Indoors. It modifies "was held.")

Notice that "indoors" comes after the verb it modifies, not before it. You would not say "Indoors she went" in normal, natural English.

"Indoors" refers to the inside of any enclosed structure — something with walls and a roof that separates the interior from the outside world. This includes:

  • A house or apartment
  • A school or office building
  • A shopping mall or store
  • A gym, stadium, or sports hall
  • A restaurant, cinema, or hospital

Importantly, "indoors" does not tell you which room or which part of the building you are in. It only tells you that you are inside a building, as opposed to being outside. The specific location within the building is irrelevant to the word's meaning.

A simple open shelter — like just a roof with no walls, or a bus stop awning — would generally not qualify as being "indoors," because "indoors" implies being fully inside an enclosed building.

The direct opposite of "indoors" is outdoors (also: outside, out of doors). "Outdoors" means in the open air, outside any building.

It was too hot to sit outdoors, so we moved indoors.

She works indoors in winter but outdoors in summer.

Keeping these two opposites in mind makes the meaning of "indoors" crystal clear: wherever "outdoors" is not, that is "indoors."

This is one of the most important things to understand about this word.

"Indoors" (with an s at the end) is the adverb. It modifies a verb.
"Indoor" (without an s) is the adjective. It modifies a noun.

Compare:

✅ We played indoors. → "Indoors" modifies the verb "played." (adverb)
✅ We played in an indoor pool. → "Indoor" modifies the noun "pool." (adjective)

✅ She stayed indoors. → "Indoors" modifies the verb "stayed." (adverb)
✅ She used an indoor treadmill. → "Indoor" modifies the noun "treadmill." (adjective)

You cannot swap these two forms. You cannot say "We played indoor" or "She used an indoors treadmill." Each form has its own job, and they are not interchangeable.

These are the most natural, frequently used patterns with "indoors":

Stay/remain indoors — a very common pairing, often used when weather or safety is a concern.

The forecast says to stay indoors today.

Go indoors — moving from outside to inside a building.

It started raining, so everyone went indoors.

Come indoors — often used as a call or invitation to enter a building.

Come indoors! Dinner is ready.

Be held/kept indoors — used for events or situations.

The match was kept indoors because of the weather.

Move/bring something indoors — transferring something from outside to inside.

We moved the plants indoors before the frost.

"Indoors" carries a sense of shelter, comfort, or safety from what is outside — especially from weather, cold, heat, or danger. When someone says "Let's go indoors," the implied message is often: let's get inside where we're protected from what's out there.

This is why you will frequently see "indoors" used in contexts involving:

  • Weather: rain, snow, extreme heat, wind
  • Health or safety: illness, pollution, danger outside
  • Comfort or preference: preferring the warmth or calm of being inside

He's not much of an outdoor person — he prefers to be indoors.
The smoke from the wildfires was so bad that authorities advised everyone to remain indoors.
"Indoors" is an adverb that means "inside a building," and it tells you where an action takes place — specifically, within an enclosed structure as opposed to out in the open air.
